uncited: Unlike [NeRF Volumetric Rendering (Coarse/Fine Sampling)](979-nerf-volumetric-rendering-coarse-fine-sampling.md) which often relies on hierarchical sampling strategies, this method performs a uniform or jittered march through the volume bounding box, evaluating the neural field on-the-fly to determine density and color at each step.
- **Input:** A trained neural volume model (MLP), camera parameters (position, orientation, field of view), transfer function, and rendering parameters (shading mode, step size, gradient step).
The neural volume is wrapped in a CUDA device class.
Template parameters define network width ($N \in \{16, 32, 64\}$) and features per level.
Provides `init()`, `launch2D()`, and `sample(p)` methods.
Supports widths from $16 \times 1$ to $16 \times 8$.
Provides `init()`, `launch()`, and `sample(p)` methods.
Initialize the ray origin and direction in world space.
-   Transform camera position to world space: `ray.org = xfmPoint(wto, camera.position)`.
-   Construct ray direction from camera forward, horizontal, and vertical vectors, shifted by normalized screen position $(screen.x - 0.5f)$ and $(screen.y - 0.5f)$, then normalized.
Intersect the ray with the volume bounding box using `intersectVolume(t0, t1, ray.org, ray.dir, self)`.
-   If no intersection is found (`!block_any(...)`), return the background color and alpha.
-   Otherwise, the ray segment of interest is $[t0, t1]$.
Iterate through the ray using an iterator `network_raymarching_iterator`.
Negate the gradient for shading purposes.
Apply opacity correction for the step size $\Delta t = t.y - t.x$.
-   If `GRADIENT_SHADING`: Transform gradient to world space $N_w = \text{xfmNormal}(otw, \nabla \text{value})$ and ray direction to world space.
Compute shaded color using `shade_scivis_light` with ambient and directional lights.
-   If `SINGLE_SHADE_HEURISTIC`: Track the point with the highest density (`highestOrg`, `highestAlpha`) encountered so far.
-   Calculate transmittance from the highest density point (`highestOrg`) to the light source using a secondary ray march `network_raymarching_transmittance` towards the light direction.
Uses hierarchical sampling with coarse and fine passes to optimize computational cost.
Choose when scene complexity varies significantly and adaptive sampling is beneficial. [Link](979-nerf-volumetric-rendering-coarse-fine-sampling.md)
Iteratively refines the ray marching path or density estimates.
Choose when high-frequency details require adaptive refinement. [Link](1494-iterative-ray-marching-with-neural-volume-inference.md)
Uses a differentiable voxel grid (DVGO) representation instead of a pure MLP.
Choose for faster inference at the cost of memory. [Link](2363-dvgo-volume-rendering-forward-pass.md)
The underlying neural network architecture used by the in-shader method. [Link](2416-mlp-with-positional-encoding.md)
Integrates radiance fields using volumetric primitives. [Link](2536-volumetric-primitive-radiance-field-integrator.md)
Tools for visualizing the ray marching process and neural network outputs. [Link](2646-neural-volume-raycasting-debug-visualization.md)
Classifies volume data using neural networks. [Link](5271-neural-network-volume-classification.md)
-   **Time Complexity:** $O(N \cdot M)$, where $N$ is the number of pixels and $M$ is the number of samples per ray.
Each sample requires a neural network inference, which is significantly more expensive than a texture lookup.
-   **Memory Complexity:** Depends on the neural network size. `TcnnDeviceVolume` and `FvsrnDeviceVolume` store the MLP weights in GPU memory.
-   **Measured Performance:** Performance is heavily dependent on the MLP width and the hardware's FP32/FP16 throughput.
Standard widths (16, 32, 64) are optimized. fV-SRN supports widths up to $16 \times 8$.
-   **Strengths:** High-quality rendering with continuous representations; supports complex shading (gradient, single-shade) directly in the shader; no need for pre-computed 3D textures.
-   **When to Use:** When high-quality, continuous volume rendering is required and computational resources allow for per-pixel neural inference.
Suitable for scientific visualization and high-fidelity rendering.
-   **When Not to Use:** When real-time performance is critical and the scene is simple enough for texture-based rendering; when memory is constrained and the MLP is large.
The framework provides a CUDA-based implementation for training and rendering neural volumes.
